item.title: Over 5,000 people in Southern Nadi struggle with water shortages, some wait 3 weeks for water trucks
item.description: More than 5,000 people in Nawai, Nawaicoba, Nalovo and surrounding areas in Southern Nadi continue to struggle with unreliable water supply, with some families waiting up to three weeks for water trucks. item.content:encoded:
More than 5,000 people in Nawai, Nawaicoba, Nalovo and surrounding areas in Southern Nadi continue to struggle with unreliable water supply, with some families waiting up to three weeks for water trucks.

This issue has been raised by Nadi resident Viliame Finau, during the Fijian Media Association Town Hall Forum at the FNU Namaka Campus Lecture Theatre in Nadi, saying that residents have been living with water cuts for years, with some having to wait between two and three weeks for water trucks to arrive.

He adds that he regularly interacts with people in these communities and the situation remains the same, with families struggling to access reliable water supply.

Finau says a network of friends is helping deliver water to communities from Nadi towards Sigatoka and Lautoka, but stresses that this cannot continue as a long-term solution.

He says some families are forced to drink salty well water as their usual water sources dry up, while others depend on water deliveries.

Finau recalls visiting a family that tells him they have still not finished the six bottles of water delivered to them a couple of weeks earlier, highlighting how carefully residents are rationing their water.

He also questions Member of Parliament and People First Party representative Rinesh Sharma about the two blue water tanks sitting on the hill at Nawaicoba, asking whether they are established by the previous FijiFirst Government.

Sharma says he entered Parliament in 2022, after FijiFirst lost the election, and cannot comment on what the previous administration did before his time.

However, he says it is the responsibility of the current Government to take forward projects left by the previous administration and ensure they are completed.

Finau then questioned the water supply arrangement involving a pipeline which he says supplies the Marriott Hotel, asking whether water from that main can be intermittently shared with surrounding communities.

He says more than 5,000 people are affected by the shortages and appeals to Government to consider their needs alongside the hotel's water requirements.

Responding to the concerns, Acting Manager Regional Operations Western of the Water Authority of Fiji, Joeli Rabuatoka says the two blue tanks at Nawaicoba are in the final stages of commissioning and are expected to help resolve water supply problems in Southern Nadi.

Rabuatoka explains that the pipeline infrastructure is already in place, but additional storage capacity is needed to cater for the population in the area.

He says the Nadi and Lautoka water systems operate through gravity supply rather than pumping, meaning water needs to be supplied from Nagado towards Nawaicoba to fill the tanks before it can flow by gravity to surrounding communities.

On the concerns about the Marriott Hotel, Rabuatoka says water supply to the hotel is scheduled for two days a week.

He says the Water Authority also considers the needs of surrounding communities and supplements their water supply through water carting.

Rabuatoka says once the two tanks are commissioned and filled, they will provide the additional storage capacity needed to improve water supply to Southern Nadi.

Finau acknowledges the work being carried out by the Water Authority but says feedback from residents indicates that water trucks are not arriving as regularly as they need them to.

He suggests that more water trucks may be required to assist communities while the major water project is being completed.

Finau also raises the possibility of introducing desalination plants in Fiji, particularly for maritime communities, referring to Papua New Guinea's preparations for desalination facilities.

He says he previously visited the District Office to raise the water concerns and contacts the Water Authority, where he is informed that communities will be connected once the major project is completed.

While welcoming the Water Authority's willingness to discuss more regular water carting, Finau maintains his plea for immediate Government intervention.

He is asking Government to consider allowing intermittent sharing of water from the pipeline supplying the Marriott Hotel to help ease the shortages faced by surrounding communities.

item.title: Kiran calls for answers over Police handling of complaints before alleged Korovou attack
item.description: Minister for Women, Children, Social Protection and Cohesion Sashi Kiran is calling for a thorough review of how Police handled earlier domestic violence complaints from a woman who was allegedly attacked with a knife by her husband in Korovou. Kiran says she is particularly concerned by allegations that the woman had an existing Domestic Violence Restraining Order (DVRO) and had repeatedly sought
item.content:encoded:
Minister for Women, Children, Social Protection and Cohesion Sashi Kiran is calling for a thorough review of how Police handled earlier domestic violence complaints from a woman who was allegedly attacked with a knife by her husband in Korovou.

Kiran says she is particularly concerned by allegations that the woman had an existing Domestic Violence Restraining Order (DVRO) and had repeatedly sought Police assistance after receiving threats to her safety.

She says reports of delays in verifying the restraining order between Police stations are deeply concerning, as such orders are intended to protect people from further violence.

The Minister stresses that when someone reports threats or a suspected breach of a restraining order, Police must respond urgently and take appropriate steps to protect the person seeking assistance.

Kiran is urging the Fiji Police Force to thoroughly review how the woman's earlier complaints were handled, how the restraining order was verified and what action was taken before the alleged attack.

She says any failures in Police response, communication or procedures must be identified and addressed to prevent similar incidents.

The Minister highlights that the Revised National Service Delivery Protocol for Responding to Cases of Gender-Based Violence, launched in July this year, outlines the responsibilities of Police officers when responding to domestic violence complaints.

She says officers are required to provide immediate assistance, arrange medical treatment where necessary, investigate complaints promptly and ensure restraining orders are properly enforced.

Kiran also reminds officers that the Fiji Police Force's No Drop Policy requires domestic violence complaints to be investigated, with appropriate action taken against alleged offenders in accordance with the law.

She stresses that Police officers must not attempt to arrange reconciliation between victims and alleged perpetrators.

The Minister is also deeply concerned by reports that the woman's daughter witnessed the alleged attack.

Kiran says children who witness domestic violence can suffer serious emotional harm and must receive appropriate protection and support.

She is urging Police and child protection agencies to work together to ensure the safety and wellbeing of children affected by domestic violence.

Kiran acknowledges that Police have confirmed the incident and that a suspect has been charged in connection with the case.

However, she stresses that the family's concerns about how earlier reports were handled must still be thoroughly examined.

The Minister says Fiji cannot continue responding to domestic violence only after people have been seriously injured or lost their lives.

She stresses that early intervention, timely Police action and accountability are essential to protecting women and children.

Kiran is also reminding women and girls experiencing domestic violence that they have the right to seek protection and support.

She is encouraging anyone who witnesses or has information about domestic violence to report it to the relevant authorities.

The National Domestic Violence Helpline 1560 is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

People experiencing domestic violence can also seek assistance from their nearest Police station, Fiji Women's Crisis Centre office or the Ministry's divisional offices.

Questions have been sent to the Fiji Police Force seeking an update on the case and a response to concerns about the handling of the woman's earlier complaints. We are awaiting their response.

item.title: Dreketi residents ask Committee to explain Constitution Bill before making submissions as they are not aware
item.description: Some residents from the interior of Dreketi are calling on the Parliamentary Special Committee to explain the Constitution Amendment Bill before they make their submissions, saying they are not fully aware of what is being proposed. The concerns were raised during the public consultation held yesterday, when a Dreketi advisory council representative spoke in Hindi to Committee member and MP Alvick
item.content:encoded:
Some residents from the interior of Dreketi are calling on the Parliamentary Special Committee to explain the Constitution Amendment Bill before they make their submissions, saying they are not fully aware of what is being proposed.

The concerns were raised during the public consultation held yesterday, when a Dreketi advisory council representative spoke in Hindi to Committee member and MP Alvick Maharaj, asking him to convey their request to the Committee.

The representative explained that some residents in the interior of Dreketi had limited information about the Bill and wanted to understand its contents before sharing their views on the proposed constitutional changes.

He also raised concerns that the Bill was written in English, which some residents have difficulty understanding.

Maharaj translated the representative's concerns to the Committee, explaining that residents were seeking a clearer understanding of the proposed changes before making their submissions.

In response, the Committee acknowledged the concerns and asked Attorney General Sevuloni Valenitabua to provide an overview of the Bill.

Valenitabua explained that the Bill proposes amendments to the 2013 Constitution and has not yet become law.

He says the Committee is conducting consultations around Fiji to hear people's views on the proposed constitutional changes.

The Attorney General also outlined several areas covered by the proposed changes, including rights relating to education, health, religion, political participation, culture, land and environmental protection.

He further explained that the proposed changes include establishing two Houses of Parliament instead of the current single-chamber system.

However, as the explanation continued, some residents still had difficulty understanding the information being presented in English.

The Committee then asked Maharaj to translate the Attorney General's explanation into Hindi, point by point, so residents could better understand the proposed changes.

The consultation continued with Maharaj translating the explanation into Hindi for those present.

item.title: Girmit digitisation project to help descendants trace ancestral roots
item.description: Descendants of Girmitiya's in Fiji could find it easier to trace their ancestral roots, with historical immigration records set to be digitised and preserved through a partnership between the Ministry of Multi-Ethnic Affairs and the National Archives of Fiji. A Memorandum of Understanding for the Girmit Digitization Project was signed today, formalising the partnership as the project moves into it
item.content:encoded:
Descendants of Girmitiya's in Fiji could find it easier to trace their ancestral roots, with historical immigration records set to be digitised and preserved through a partnership between the Ministry of Multi-Ethnic Affairs and the National Archives of Fiji.

A Memorandum of Understanding for the Girmit Digitization Project was signed today, formalising the partnership as the project moves into its second phase.

Permanent Secretary for Multi-Ethnic Affairs Dr Vinesh Kumar says the project will help descendants find out who their forefathers were, where they came from, when they arrived in Fiji and the circumstances that brought them to the country.

Kumar says approximately 60,537 Indians arrived in Fiji under the indenture system between 1879 and 1960.

He says historical documents, including immigration passes, passenger registers and plantation assignments, contain valuable information about individual identities, family histories and ancestral origins.

Kumar says Phase One of the project has been successfully completed, establishing the database structure, backing up existing digital records and developing initial applications connected to the database.

He says the database has been designed to accommodate more than 60,000 Girmitiya records.

Under the MOU, the Ministry will lead the implementation of the database and in-house digitisation process, while the National Archives will provide archival expertise and guidance to ensure the historical materials are handled and preserved according to appropriate archival standards.

Permanent Secretary for Information and National Archives Eseta Nadakuitavuki says the agreement formalises the partnership as the project moves into Phase Two, focusing on the digitisation and long-term preservation of the historical collection.

Nadakuitavuki says the National Archives of Fiji remains the sole statutory custodian of all original records, and all master digital files will be formally transferred to the Archives for permanent preservation.

She says the Ministry will provide a specialised large-format book scanner, computers and a server to support the digitisation work.

Nadakuitavuki says the scanner will be permanently transferred to the National Archives upon completion of the project, strengthening its capacity to digitise other national collections in the future.

Dr Kumar says the MOU does not have a fixed end date and will remain in force for the duration of the Indian labour records digitisation project.

He says the agreement may be reviewed every three years to reflect changes in project requirements and institutional responsibilities.

Kumar says there is also potential for the two institutions to explore the digitisation and preservation of historical records relating to other multi-ethnic communities in Fiji.
